title-group.article-title: The Long-Term Mental Health Impact of Disasters: A Systematic Review and Multilevel Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Epidemiological Studies

abstract.p: Scientific research on the mental health effects of disasters has primarily focused on short-term consequences. This review aims to provide a long-term perspective, examining multiple contributing factors simultaneously. We registered this review (PROSPERO 2020, CRD42020108528), and searched Medline, PsycInfo, PTSDpubs, Web of Science, and SocINDEX from inception to July 2024. After screening 33,205 titles and abstracts, we extracted epidemiological longitudinal data from 71 studies, with up to six waves and a total of 137,004 participants. Disaster type (natural/human-made), category (e.g., earthquakes, floods, terrorist attacks), mental health outcome (e.g., posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety), population type (children/adolescents, adults), disaster year, measurement month, study quality, and country income were included in a multilevel meta-analysis. Pooled average prevalence of current or recent mental health problems was 22.1% (95% CI [10.95–39.57]). When controlling for the other factors, prevalence did not differ by disaster type, category, mental health outcome, population type, year, study quality, or country income. Despite high heterogeneity, the mental health burden in exposed populations decreased from month 1 to 300 after an initial peak in the first months, followed by a second peak after approximately a decade, before declining again (p<0.001). Mental health burdens post-disaster may be more universally distributed than previously believed. Earlier studies identifying gradual post-disaster recovery may have underestimated the long-term effects. The analysis revealed a shortage of high-quality studies with measurements beyond four years. The topic requires further investigation with consistently repeated measurements at standard intervals to confirm the presence and early predictors of both larger and smaller peaks.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Populations have been confronted with disasters and major devastating events for as long as people have populated Earth. Although the exact number of natural and human-induced disasters, coupled with future prevalence, remains a topic of debate, societies varyingly confront floods, fires, earthquakes, technological disasters, terrorism, and mass violence.1–3 A combination of climate change, population growth, humanitarian crises, conflict, and war can potentially exacerbate the effects of such events.2 Although precise developments remain uncertain, new events involving loss of life, damage, and destruction are highly probable, and such events entail detrimental consequences for societies as a whole. The mental health effects of disaster exposure have been examined systematically for decades, resulting in a variety of overview studies. For example, there are studies that focus specifically on changes in occurrence of a particular mental health outcome (e.g., posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD], depression, or suicide),4–9 type of disaster (natural or human-made),10 or disaster event category (e.g., earthquake, flood, terrorist attack, shooting).8–11 Some reviews have synthesized findings on multiple aspects.12–16

Review of this literature reveals certain patterns. First, disaster exposure may have a substantial influence on mental health and psychopathology,4,5,9,12–15 with the number of human casualties playing a relevant role (i.e., effect size is strongly related to death rate or injury).4,12 Prevalence has been established as higher after the disaster compared to before,9,10 and higher in exposed versus unexposed comparison groups.7,10

Second, time since the disaster event is a verified relevant factor. Longer duration is associated with lower effect-size estimates.12,13,15,16 As summarized in one review: “A few exceptions notwithstanding, the general rule was for samples to improve as time passed.”13

Third, mental health problems like PTSD, depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and suicidality are typical, but only in a relatively small minority of exposed individuals.4,13,15,16 Severe mental health problems in adults and chronic symptom elevation in youth beyond the first months usually do not occur in more than 30% of exposed populations.15,16 Disasters also produce multiple outcome patterns. Labels like “resilient,” “recovery,” “delayed onset,” or “chronic” have been assigned to such patterns or trajectories. The first two labels are most prevalent. Often, the majority of those exposed experience only transient distress and maintain a stable trajectory of healthy functioning or resilience. Some survivors recover within months, or one or two years.15 Such trajectories tend to differ per disorder.16

Fourth, prior reviews describe mixed findings concerning the importance of differences among disaster types and categories and how they affect the mental health of those exposed. Some authors find higher impairment for natural disasters,7,12 earthquakes in particular,16 and others higher for human-made disasters,4 mass violence, and industrial disasters among specific categories.13,16

Fifth, disaster scholars describe a wide range of risk and protective factors, focusing on degree of exposure at the individual, community, and society levels (e.g., confrontation with death, danger and injury, gender, age, ethnicity, personality traits, preexisting health, actual and perceived social support, ties with others, resources and resource loss, secondary stressors, and cultural and socioeconomic contexts).4–8,12–15,17,18

Sixth, and most critically, there is a dearth of long-term and longitudinal research, a shortcoming consistently mentioned in available systematic reviews.4–6,8,11,13,19 Length of follow-up is also limited among studies that include some durational findings. In two recent meta-analyses, by Bonde and colleagues7 and Beaglehole and colleagues,10 timelines were primarily restricted to 24 and 48 months, respectively; they did not examine long-term effects. While highly informative in many respects, the systematic review by Newnham and colleagues,16 which compares mental health trajectories across different disaster categories, considers the long-term as just one time frame: longer than 24 months.

We conducted a search in Medline (Ovid), PsycInfo (Ovid), PTSDpubs (formerly PILOTS: Published International Literature on Traumatic Stress), ProQuest, Web of Science, and SocINDEX (EBSCOhost) in August 2024 using the search terms: review OR meta-analysis OR systematic review AND disasters AND long-term OR long term OR lasting OR longitudinal. Based on the reviews mentioned and this search, we conclude that no systematic review or meta-analysis has assessed the long-term effects of disaster exposure across different time periods while controlling for multiple characteristics that potentially affect mental health risks.

In summary, available reviews consistently highlight the serious mental health effects of disasters and related trajectories. They also frequently highlight factors that determine risk and vulnerability for affected populations across diverse disaster categories, both natural and human-made. At the same time, they point toward a major lacuna regarding long-term influence. This multilevel meta-analytic review aims to shed light on disaster-related long-term mental health effects and progression, taking into account relevant contextual predictors and control variables. The focus is on a broad range of mental (not physical) health outcomes (e.g., PTSD, depression, anxiety, suicidality, substance abuse, panic disorder) measured repeatedly along the post-disaster timeline. We combine multiple characteristics that potentially affect mental health risks in a controlled analysis: disaster type (natural or human-made), category (e.g., earthquake, flood, etc.), population type (children and adolescents, adults), disaster year (more recent or longer ago), socioeconomic context (country income level), and study features (study quality, hierarchical levels within the data).

sec.title: Databases and publication year
sec.p: We searched Medline (Ovid), PsycInfo (Ovid), PTSDpubs (formerly PILOTS: Published International Literature on Traumatic Stress), ProQuest, Web of Science, and SocINDEX (EBSCOhost) for study abstracts published from inception to July 2024 for English-language studies.

sec.title: Search terms
sec.p: We categorized keywords according to the Population Exposure Outcome model to which we added a method cluster: Population: victims, survivors; Exposure: disaster, catastrophes, environmental hazard, epidemics, accidents, terrorism; Outcome: mental health, psychosocial complaints, stress, distress, psychiatric disorders, anxiety/stress disorders, mood disorders, PTSD, substance abuse, depression (expanding search terms from reviews by Norris and colleagues13 and Bonde and colleagues7); Method: cohort, longitudinal, prospective, systematic review, meta-analysis.20 (The search terms per database are included in Supplemental Data File 2, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A253.) Given the large number of studies to screen (N = 33,205), we did not take measures to find additional studies.

sec.title: Guidelines and registration
sec.p: This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We conducted our search in Covidence, and pre-registered the review in Prospero (2020, CRD42020108528).

sec.title: Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria
sec.p: We included articles published in English-language peer-reviewed journals that contained full-text reports of quantitative studies assessing disaster effects. As what constitutes a disaster is not always clear, we defined the term specifically to denote acute, collectively experienced events with sudden onset.13 (See also Supplemental Data File 1, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A254.) Following categorization of search terms, we formulated inclusion and exclusion criteria.

sec.title: Population
sec.p: Population-level inclusion criteria encompassed exposed adults, children, and adolescents (<18) of nonclinical populations who were directly (e.g., survivors of an accident or earthquake) or indirectly (e.g., living in disaster region) affected by a disaster. Exclusion criteria included professionals or responders and those not living in the vicinity of a disaster, as well as victims of war and armed conflict.

sec.title: Exposure
sec.p: Exposure inclusion criteria comprised disaster exposure that affected a group and had an external cause (e.g., not mass suicide) and disasters that occurred at a workplace where the event happened to occur (e.g., terrorist attack, school shooting). Exclusion criteria included studies assessing the effects of multiple disasters within one sample or measurements from long-term single-disaster studies since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic (to avoid contamination of findings by pandemic-related threats, losses, and stressors).

sec.title: Outcome
sec.p: Inclusion criteria encompassed studies containing mental health outcomes as measured via questionnaire, interview, or medical records regarding individual prevalence of mental health disorder (e.g., depression, anxiety, distress, PTSD, anxiety disorder, substance abuse, or suicidality). Exclusion criteria involved studies reporting health effects (stress-related) limited to physical symptoms (e.g., brain injury, medically unexplained symptoms), post-disaster interventions, mental health utilization, positive outcomes (e.g., posttraumatic growth), and psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia).

sec.title: Method
sec.p: Inclusion criteria entailed longitudinally designed studies with two or more post-disaster assessments of the same sample: measurement durations not longer than three months, with measurement intervals of at least three months. The last measurement had to be at least 12 months post-event and outcome measures had to be comparable across assessments. Studies needed to encompass at least 30 participants at baseline who experienced the disaster. The design excluded studies that developed a methodology or instrument or that contained an intervention, as well as studies that did not use the same methodology or instrument across all measurements. Studies with outcomes reported by an ancillary, unprofessional person (e.g., a parent or caregiver) were also excluded. Additionally, we did not include studies with only continuous scores (e.g., means and standard deviations) and studies with poor methodological quality. (See the quality assessment section.)

sec.title: Screening Procedure
sec.p: Titles and abstracts were divided and independently screened by two authors. Disagreements were discussed until we reached consensus. If necessary, a third person was consulted. When in doubt about a title/abstract, the article was retained for the full text stage. For manuscripts based on the same dataset, we included the first published article unless a subsequent paper measured more relevant mental health variables or included more assessment waves. If the more recent paper did not measure all variables assessed in the first published paper, we included both. We only used mental health variables from the initial paper, however, that were not measured in the later one. Studies that did not appear to meet all inclusion criteria when fully reviewed, and studies that did not report useful statistics for the mental health variables (e.g., if the variable was only displayed in graphs but not statistics) were excluded.

sec.title: Quality Assessment
sec.p: We conducted an assessment of study quality using an adapted version of the Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies from the Effective Public Health Practice Project.21 This assessment included criteria such as selection bias, study design, data collection methods, withdrawal, and dropout. Additionally, one item from the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort studies was incorporated to assess outcome quality.22 A study with no poor scores was considered strong, while those with up to two poor scores were deemed moderate. We excluded studies with three or more poor scores. (Supplemental Data File 3, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A255 contains more information on quality assessment per study.)

sec.title: Data Extraction
sec.p: From the included papers, we extracted available information on: disaster type and category, year, country, and region of disaster occurrence, population age (i.e., adult, children and adolescents, or all ages), relevant mental health outcomes observed (e.g., PTSD, depression, suicidality), number of assessments conducted (measurement waves), month of measurement (in cases with multiple measurement months, the last month was taken), type of instrument used, total sample size per wave (denominator), and number of participants with a mental health problem per wave (numerator). We calculated prevalence based on the numerator and denominator. The distinction between disorders and symptoms was not always consistent among different authors. We applied the term probable when used by the authors or when the study employed a validated screening or assessment questionnaire with recommended cut-off values. (See Supplemental Data File 6, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A256.) This was especially relevant for PTSD, posttraumatic stress (PTS), and distress. Data extraction started on 26 May 2020. Data were extracted by two authors (MD and AB) and three assistants, and were later double-checked. We clustered countries based on World Bank income categories (high, upper-middle, lower-middle, and low income).

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: We used a multilevel (meta-analysis) logit-logistic regression model to generate pooled estimates of mental health problems in the disaster timeline.23–25 This type of analysis enabled us to distinguish between fixed and random effects. Fixed effects capture specific characteristics that remain constant across outcomes, while random effects account for variability and differences among clustered outcomes. Clustering applies to hierarchical levels (observations, measurement waves, studies, and countries), as well as mental health problems and disaster categories. (Figure 1 displays the data’s multilevel structure.)

caption.p: Multilevel data structure. Note: In the dataset, six hierarchical levels can be distinguished. Level 1 (“observations”) captures the prevalence of a specific mental health outcome for a distinct sample at a specific post-disaster time point. Observations are grouped into Level 2 (“measurement waves”), representing each follow-up time within a study. Multiple waves belong to the same study (Level 3). Studies are further grouped by country (Level 4), disaster category (Level 5), and outcome type (Level 6). The data therefore follow a cross-classified structure.

sec.p: As a first step, we estimated the effect of several factors on the overall average prevalence of mental health problems (similar to the overall rate in other forms of meta-analysis). As a second step, we estimated average prevalence of mental health problems per disaster category (e.g., earthquake, flood, shooting), disaster type (natural or human-made), country income group (low to high), population type (children/adolescents, adults, all ages), study quality (moderate or high), outcome category (type of mental health issue), and month.

sec.title: Fixed effects
sec.p: We included month (time since disaster; modeled with linear, quadratic, and cubic components; see also Norris and colleagues13), disaster year, population type (children/adolescents, adults, all ages), disaster type (natural or human-made), study quality (moderate or high), and country income group (low to high) as fixed effects in the model.

sec.title: Random effects
sec.p: The model consisted of six levels. Level 1 denoted individual prevalence per outcome from each observed population; at this level, we modeled binomial error variance (constrained to 1). Level 2 modeled variance between measurement waves within studies. Level 3 accounted for variance among studies, and Level 4 among countries. We included variance among disaster categories and outcome types as cross-classified Levels 5 and 6, respectively (Figure 1).

All fixed effects (months since disaster, disaster year, population type, disaster type, study quality, and country income) and random effects (six levels) were estimated simultaneously in a single model. Thus, we controlled effect estimates for the other effects in the model.

All models were estimated in MLwiN version 3.01 using restricted iterative generalized least squares with first-order penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL). The overall pooled prevalence of mental health problems was equally weighted for the fixed effects factors and categories within a factor (indicator scoring [0,1] minus 1/N[cat], N[cat] = number of categories in factor). No weight was added for sample size differences (often implemented in meta-analyses), primarily because heterogeneity among individual observations and studies was so large that weighting for sample size would make the different model estimates significantly more difficult to interpret.

sec.title: Characteristics of Included Studies
sec.p: The literature search retrieved a total of 33,205 records to screen. After initially reviewing the records, we identified 783 papers requiring full-text review. Eventually, 71 studies, published from 1990 to 2024, were included for data extraction.26–96 (See the flowchart in Supplemental Data File 4, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A257.) The average baseline female sex proportion, extracted from 68 studies was 54.03% (95% CI [51.04-57.02]). (See Supplemental Data File 7, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A258.)

The studies addressed disasters in 23 countries from four World Health Organization regions; almost half of the studies focused on China (including Taiwan) and the United States (34); Americas: Colombia (2), Honduras (1), Mexico (1), United States (8); Europe: Armenia (2), Croatia (1), France (2), Greece (1), Iceland (1), Netherlands (4), Norway (5), Spain (2), Sweden (3), United Kingdom (1); Southeast Asia: India (1), Indonesia (1), Nepal (1), Thailand (2); Western Pacific: Australia (1), China (26; 2 of which were from Taiwan, a high-income area), Japan (3), South Korea (2). (See Supplemental Data File 5, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A259 for a world map.) Nearly all studies investigated populations in high-income (35) and upper-middle-income countries (32); three studies addressed disasters in lower-middle-income countries, and one study followed up with survivors across countries from different income groups.

Most of the studied disasters took place in the year 2000 or later (55 of 71 studies; the first disaster took place in 1985, the last in 2017) and the majority concerned natural disasters (48 compared to 23 human-made). The 71 studies included 76 samples, covering multiple disaster categories: earthquakes (29), storms (e.g., cyclones and snowstorms) (9), terrorist attacks (9), tsunamis (8), accidents (6), floods (4), shootings (4), explosions (3), volcanic eruptions (2), fires (1), and landslides (1). The majority of studies were of moderate quality (53). The mental health outcomes differed: PTSD (43), depression (26), PTS (18), other (e.g., agoraphobia, dysthymia) (14), anxiety (11), sleep problems (11), distress (5), panic disorder (4), substance abuse (4), grief (2), and suicidality (2). Since several studies focused on multiple outcomes, the total number of measurement series adds up to 140. As Table 1 displays, these 140 measurement series included 403 observations divided over six waves: the first wave included 140 observations (38.64%; n = 52,937), the second wave included 140 observations (35.65%; n = 48,844), the third wave included 76 observations (14.57%; n = 19,964), the fourth wave included 40 observations (7.28%; n = 9,979), the fifth wave included 6 observations (2.85%; n = 3,911), and the sixth wave included 1 observation (1.00%; n = 1,369). Half (49.88%) of the observations were recorded within 12 months of the disaster and 93.05% within 48 months. (Supplemental Data Files 6, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A256 and 7, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A258 provide additional information for each study.)

sec.title: Mental Health Problems: Prevalence, Determinants, and Variation
sec.p: Table 2 presents results from the multilevel analysis. In the fixed effects analysis, the mental health burden in populations confronted with disasters changes across time (p<0.001). With other factors taken into account, prevalence does not differ among natural and human-made disasters, general age, or country income groups, nor is disaster year or study quality an influence. For the random effects analysis, we observed substantial between-measurement and between-study variance, as well as between-disaster categories and mental health outcomes. The pooled prevalence of current or recent mental health problems was 22.1% (95% CI [10.95–39.57]), yet the analysis indicates extensive heterogeneity underlying this estimate, both across and within studies. No prevalence estimates covered a time period longer than 12 months.

sec.p: Figure 2 provides an overview of the stratified pooled prevalence estimates of post-disaster mental health problems, with 95% CI for each mental health outcome, disaster category and type, population age group, study quality level, and country income group, controlled for the other factors.

Note: Pooled prevalence estimates are controlled for: time, disaster type, disaster year, population, study quality, and country income (fixed effects), as well as measurement wave, study, country, mental health outcome, and disaster category (random effects). The total number of observations with assigned country income is 397 out of 403. (Survivors of one aircraft disaster were followed up in different countries.)

sec.p: Figure 3 illustrates that the time effect (shown in Table 2) does not follow a straight linear trend; rather, it better fits a polynomial trend line. The decrease in the first few years is followed by an increase, peaking between 110 and 220 months (approximately 9–18 years), followed by a rather steep decrease. This graph also shows that most available data cover the first quarter of the timeline.

caption.p: Pooled prevalence of post-disaster mental health problems by month. Note: The figure shows the pooled average prevalence of mental health problems with CIs per month since the disaster. Estimates are controlled for disaster type, disaster year, population, study quality, and country income (fixed effects); and measurement wave, study, country, mental health outcome, and disaster category (random effects).

sec.p: It was not possible to systematically compare prevalence in disaster-exposed populations to a control group. Only three of the 71 studies in our dataset contain control group measurements (19 of 403 observations).41,57,89 The analysis demonstrates a higher average prevalence of 27.6% (95% CI: 22.60–32.60; n = 19) in disaster-exposed populations compared to 13.82% (95% CI: 9.03–18.71; n =19) in the control group (Two-Sample T-Test, p < 0.0001). Without adjustment for other factors, this suggests that the pooled prevalence in exposed populations is higher than in unexposed populations.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: We conducted this review with the objective of better understanding the long-term mental health effects of disasters, a lacuna identified in the international disaster mental health literature. By conducting a multilevel meta-analysis, controlling for multiple factors simultaneously, we estimated the pooled prevalence of current or recent mental health problems at 22.1% (95% CI [10.95–39.57]). Although our analysis revealed extensive heterogeneity across and within studies, we clearly found that a substantial proportion of people affected by disasters experiences mental health problems of one type or another. We verified the well-established effects disasters have in the first months and years on the mental health of affected populations. In large part, other disaster mental health reviews and meta-analyses confined their investigations to a relatively short time frame, typically spanning two to four years,7,10,16 or compared post-disaster measurements with predisaster or control groups.9,10 The broad time frame of our analysis, spanning 1–300 months, distinguishes our review. Our controlled evaluation demonstrates significant fluctuations over time. We found that, after initial improvement, a gradual increase in mental health problems generally follows, potentially peaking again years after a disaster.

Another noteworthy finding concerns the differences among event types. Arguably, the classic, conceptual dichotomy between natural and human-made disasters and their inherent causes is becoming less clear. Natural disasters such as floods and storms can have a human cause (climate change) or be exacerbated by human interference (pollution, communities near rivers and coastlines), further complicating reflections on whether events were preventable and/or caused by negligence or even malign intent. We found no significant differences in mental health outcome between natural and human-made disasters, contrary to the conclusions of other authors.12,13 Similarly, we did not find significant distinctions in effects among disaster categories, such as earthquakes, mass violence, and industrial disasters.12,13,16

One underexplored issue is how cultural and socioeconomic contexts influence mental health outcomes of disasters. Norris and colleagues13,14 found higher prevalence of deleterious mental health post-disaster in developing countries. They speculated that how disasters are assessed in different socioeconomic contexts may have influenced their findings; less severe disasters are more often studied in developed countries, while studies from developing countries may be limited to more severe disasters. Unfortunately, the absence of low-income countries and the small number of lower-middle-income countries in our reviewed studies did not allow us to thoroughly explore this theme. More research is needed to understand how cultural and socioeconomic contexts influence the mental health effects of disasters, both in manifestation and assessment. Although lower prevalence of poor mental health in lower-income contexts aligns with country-level studies showing a positive relationship between wealth and mental impairment,97–101 the predictive value of context is unlikely to eclipse the importance of disaster exposure level and other potentially traumatic events.97,98

When considering directions for further research, it is important to emphasize Norris and colleagues’14 warning not to unnecessarily burden study participants and waste scarce resources on redundant investigations: “We will state our opinion unequivocally that we do not need more research that establishes only that severely exposed disaster victims develop psychological disorders or, worse, that barely exposed disaster victims do not. We need carefully conceived and theory-driven studies of basic process that are longitudinal in design.” Based on our preliminary results, we concur and reemphasize the importance of long-term over short-term research.

The current study has several strengths worth noting. We conducted research using an extensive predefined search strategy and applied stringent inclusion criteria and comparability standards. By integrating data from a wide range of studies with a sizable number of participants, we were able to conduct the first multilevel meta-analytic review on the mental health effects of disasters, controlling for multiple factors simultaneously. We also excluded measurements potentially contaminated by the global COVID-19 pandemic. Only one study by Hikichi and colleagues50 included a final follow-up measurement during the pandemic; we excluded this measurement from the meta-analysis.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Notable study limitations include restriction to English-language studies, the possibility of missing relevant studies (despite identifying a vast number of records through the search), and exclusion of continuous outcomes from our analysis. Additionally, though our range of mental health problems is similar to earlier reviews,12,13,15,16 it is not exhaustive (for instance, psychotic disorders are excluded), and certain mental health outcomes, particularly PTSD, may be overrepresented. Moreover, not all assessments constitute clinical diagnoses. It is likely that a portion of study participants already had mental health problems before experiencing respective disasters.15 The selective nature of outcomes—ranging from clinical diagnoses and probable disorders to trauma-related symptoms and subjective experiences of distress—further complicates the longitudinal comparability of mental health outcomes, even though we found no significant differences among outcome types. In addition, cross-cultural differences and variations in data collection methods, diagnostic criteria, assessment instruments, and assessment timeframes pose potential biases. Likewise, our dataset only includes a portion of countries and regions, represents a limited number of lower-middle-income countries, and lacks low-income countries. (See Supplemental Data File 5, https://links.lww.com/HRP/A259.) This may affect the generalizability of the findings.

Each measured mental health outcome reflects a unique combination of characteristics linked to, among other things, the disaster, affected population, point in time, methodology used, and cultural and socioeconomic context, all contributing to heterogeneity. Our analysis is a first effort in considering multiple factors simultaneously. Nevertheless, we can extend and optimize our approach. Unfortunately, we were unable to include more risk and protective factors in the meta-analysis. In an attempt to include female sex, a confirmed risk factor for post-disaster mental health,12,13,15 the baseline female sex proportion was not a reliable proxy for follow-up measurements.

Perhaps the most significant limitation, given our objective, was the limited availability of post-disaster measurements exceeding 48 months (6.95% of observations; 16 of 71 studies). Thus, we need to exercise caution in drawing firm conclusions about the shape of long-term trends. In the data on which Figure 3 is based, there are 11 measurements between 72 and 144 months (six to twelve years). In 8 of these, prevalence is higher than before 72 months, producing the second peak. All 8 measurements are from the last wave of their respective measurement series—the studies end at that point, with no follow-up measurements. Beyond 144 months, and up to 300 months (13–25 years), we found 9 observations. Each was preceded by at least 1 measurement before, but not in, the 72–144-month period. In every case, prevalence decreased during this time frame. These particularities are relevant for two reasons. First, we cannot determine how the trend continued in populations contributing to the second peak, since measurement stopped at that point. Second, the few studies with the longest follow-up (up to 300 months) do not sufficiently unpack the prevalence changes in the large middle area of the timeline. Longer-duration measurements with periodic follow-ups are essential to fill gaps and improve the accuracy of estimates. Such longer durations are also necessary to determine more detailed trajectories or response courses, as repeatedly recommended in the literature.4,8,16,19

There is a need for long-term research across diverse geographies and cultural and socioeconomic contexts, as well as for additional syntheses addressing the identified limitations. These needs extend beyond the scope of this review. While we deliberately excluded pandemics, virus outbreaks, war, and armed conflict, these events significantly affect thousands of people worldwide as well, and studies confirm attendant mental health effects.7,102,103 Therefore, their long-term influences, which may follow similar patterns to natural and human-made disasters, also warrant careful scholarly attention.

sec.title: Implications
sec.p: The accumulated body of knowledge on the mental health burden of disasters provides an invaluable starting point for public health and safety authorities, health care professionals, and other responders to prepare and implement preventive measures, mitigation strategies, or curative interventions across the disaster timeline. Our review, however, urges caution in forming firm general conclusions. Notably, we must make assumptions about differences in mental health risks according to disaster type or category with care. Further, the nature of disaster-related threats and losses, as well as vulnerability profiles of affected populations, can differ greatly across disaster settings, and thus, must be taken into account. Finally, perhaps the most profound practical implication is that, by relying on gradual post-disaster mental health improvement, we may have underestimated the long-term effects. The observed rise in mental health problems years after a disaster, suggests a “twin peaks” phenomenon. Nonetheless, given gaps in data beyond four years, the presence of multiple peaks is poorly understood, requiring validation and conscientious interpretation. In this context, it is notable that the increase identified in the combined longitudinal samples corresponds with findings from a systematic review of PTSD following the 9/11 terrorist attacks in New York City. This study reported declining mental health for responders and residents five to six years post-9/11.8

It is important to better understand the combination of factors and the dynamics that contribute to mental health risks at later points in time. A cascading interplay of risk factors, reflected, for instance, in accumulated unmet health care needs, unresolved and new problems, life events, lack of support, and secondary stressors in the aftermath, may account for the increased mental health burden.17 In the years following a disaster, social relationships can deteriorate,15,18 and those affected may experience diminished recognition within their personal, professional, and community environments. The explanations described in the literature align with the factors identified by the authors of the included studies, who link them to elevated levels of mental health problems. For example, Tajima and colleagues86 highlight major property loss, the death of a colleague, life-threatening danger, and discrimination or slurs as factors that contribute to long-term problem drinking. Goenjian and colleagues47 attribute their findings to two post-disaster risk factors: chronic conditions (i.e., newly reported hypertension, diabetes, and arthritis) and adverse conditions in the earthquake zone (including lack of heat, electricity, housing, transportation, and destruction of physical and community infrastructure). Finally, Lima and colleagues68 emphasize the difficult living conditions in affected communities: “This may be due to the continued stressful environment in which our subjects lived as they waited to be resettled in neighbouring towns that did not welcome this influx.”

Beyond initial effects and despite extensive restoration efforts (e.g., repair of housing, infrastructure, schools, shops, and businesses), these examples and our review suggest that a substantial portion of the population in disaster-affected communities continues experiencing a mental health burden—largely invisible in scientific reporting until now, and more universal in nature than previously assumed. Such burden is part of the persistent lingering effects of disasters that, as described by Bonanno and colleagues,15 transcends the individual: “Disasters affect the nature and structure of families. They impact the communities in which they take place, taxing their institutions and sometimes challenging their survival. The impact of a disaster can also ripple through larger segments of a society and sometimes alter the lives of people in remote regions far removed from the geographic loci of the event.” These potentially broad and enduring influences underscore the need for early, proactive, participation-driven recovery approaches. With support from long-term monitoring programs to guide shared decision-making, we can target at-risk communities to help alleviate the mental health burdens of disasters.
